A.explanation: Gives $9.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ W}$, about one-third of the kinetic energy gained per second, so it underestimates the work done in $0.020 \text{ s}$.

B.explanation: Gives $1.8 \times 10^{-2} \text{ W}$, smaller than $\frac{1}{2}mv^2/t$ for $m = 1.2 \times 10^{-4} \text{ kg}$ and $v = 3.0 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, so it underestimates the energy transferred.

C.explanation: Equals the gain in kinetic energy $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$ divided by $0.020 \text{ s}$, giving about $2.7 \times 10^{-2} \text{ W}$.

D.explanation: Gives $37 \text{ W}$, about a thousand times too large, caused by failing to convert the mass from $0.12 \text{ g}$ to kilograms.

hints: Notice the mass is $0.12 \text{ g}$, the take-off velocity is $3.0 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and the push time is $0.020 \text{ s}$ - convert the mass to $\text{kg}$ first.
Connect the leg work to energy: the legs give the grasshopper kinetic energy $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$ at take-off.
Next divide that kinetic energy in joules by the $0.020 \text{ s}$ contact time because average power is $P = W/t$.
walkthrough: Convert mass to SI units: $m = 0.12 \text{ g} = 0.12 \times 10^{-3} \text{ kg} = 1.2 \times 10^{-4} \text{ kg}$.
State the energy transferred by the legs as kinetic energy at leaving the ground: $E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$.
Substitute $m = 1.2 \times 10^{-4} \text{ kg}$ and $v = 3.0 \text{ m s}^{-1}$: $E_k = 0.5 \times 1.2 \times 10^{-4} \times (3.0)^2 = 5.4 \times 10^{-4} \text{ J}$.
Use average power $P = W/t$ with $W \approx E_k$ and $t = 0.020 \text{ s}$: $P = 5.4 \times 10^{-4} / 0.020$.
Calculate $P = 2.7 \times 10^{-2} \text{ W}$ with unit $\text{J s}^{-1} = \text{W}$. This is option C.
